issues.legal_issue: A village office involving appointment and control by the State is an office under the State for purposes of the guarantee of equal opportunity in public employment.
material_facts: The village officer was appointed by the Collector, and the State granted or continued the office’s emoluments.
The Collector could discipline, suspend, remove, or dismiss the officer, and the Board of Revenue could prescribe qualifications for appointment.
The village officer performed public duties, including revenue, magistrate, civil, and police functions.
issues.conclusion: The village office was an office under the State.
issues.legal_principle: The expression “office under the State” in Article 16(1) and (2) bears its natural meaning and is not restricted by the provisions governing civil services in Part XIV. The Court relied on M. Ramappa v. Sangappa, which treated village offices filled by government appointment as offices under the Government.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_challenges_public_appointment and state_appoints_office and state_controls_holder and state_provides_remuneration and office_involves_public_duties

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenges_public_ap: A person brought a constitutional writ challenging an appointment to a public office.
predicates.state_appoints_office: A State authority appoints the holder of the office.
predicates.state_controls_holder: A State authority has disciplinary or other control over the office holder.
predicates.state_provides_remuneration: The State provides or continues the remuneration attached to the office.
predicates.office_involves_public_duties: The office holder performs duties on behalf of the public or the State.
predicates.office_is_under_state: The office is an office under the State for purposes of equal opportunity in public employment.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenges a public appointment and the State appoints and controls the holder, provides remuneration, and the office involves public duties, the office is under the State.

issues.legal_issue: The guarantee of equal opportunity in public employment applies to a hereditary public office when its emoluments are attached to the office rather than held as independent pre-existing property.
material_facts: The emoluments attached to the village office could consist of land, revenue assignments, fees, salary, or other remuneration granted or continued by the State.
The emoluments went with the office and were not a separate family property right independent of the office.
The Act allowed a person to sue to establish entitlement to the office or its emoluments, but that did not establish an independent property right to the emoluments.
issues.conclusion: The hereditary character of the office did not take it outside Article 16; the guarantee applied to the office.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished shebaitship, discussed in Angurbala Mullick v. Debabrata Mullick and Kalipada Chakraborti v. Palani Bala Devi, as property of a peculiar character. It relied on Venkata v. Rama and Musti Venkata Jagannada Sharma v. Musti Veerabhadrayya for the principle that emoluments are an appanage of the village office, not family property independent of it. Manubolu Ranga Reddi v. Maram Reddi Dasaradharami recognized an enforceable family right under the Act, but did not establish an independent property right to emoluments. The Court also noted the differing views in Ramachandurani Purshotham v. Ramachandurani Venkatappa, Pasala Rama Rao v. Board of Revenue, and Chandra Chowdary v. Board of Revenue, and held that nothing about the nature of the office excluded it from Article 16(1) and (2).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_concerns_public: A constitutional challenge concerns appointment to a public office.
predicates.office_emoluments_attached_to_office: The remuneration is attached to and passes with the office.
predicates.independent_property_right_to_emoluments: A person or family has a property right to the remuneration independent of holding the office.
predicates.equal_opportunity_guarantee_applies_to_o: The equal opportunity guarantee applies to appointment to the office.

issues.definition: If a constitutional challenge concerns a public office whose remuneration is attached to the office and is not an independent property right, the equal opportunity guarantee applies to that office.

issues.legal_issue: A selection rule that gives preference in appointment to a public office solely on the basis of descent violates the prohibition on discrimination in public employment.
material_facts: A village was divided into two villages, the existing village offices ceased, and new offices were created.
The governing rule directed the Collector to choose persons for the new offices from among the families of the last holders.
The authorities selected the son of the former village officer as the nearest heir and rejected the petitioner’s claim, expressly relying on the hereditary principle.
issues.conclusion: The rule discriminated on the ground of descent alone and was void to that extent; the appointment orders based on it were set aside, and the application had to be considered on its merits without applying that principle.
issues.legal_principle: Article 16(1) guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment, and Article 16(2) prohibits discrimination on the ground of descent in respect of employment or office under the State. Under Article 13(1), a pre-Constitution law is void to the extent that it is inconsistent with fundamental rights. Article 16(4) was not at issue, and the Court expressed no opinion on its scope.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_public_appoi: A constitutional challenge is brought against a decision appointing a person to a public office.
predicates.appointment_selection_uses_descent_alone: The selection rule makes family descent the basis for choosing candidates.
predicates.descent_preference_affects_candidate: The descent-based preference affects a candidate’s opportunity to obtain the office.
predicates.descent_based_selection_rule_invalid_to_: The descent-based selection rule is invalid to the extent that it discriminates on the ground of descent.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge to a public appointment shows that descent alone governs selection and affects a candidate’s opportunity, the descent-based selection rule is invalid to the extent of that discrimination.

issues.legal_issue: A candidate who applied for a public office may challenge an adverse appointment decision made by applying a descent-based rule, where the candidate’s right to apply did not depend on that rule.
material_facts: The petitioner applied for the newly created village office and was initially appointed by the Revenue Divisional Officer.
On appeal, the petitioner’s appointment was displaced in favour of the son of the former office holder on the express basis of the hereditary principle.
The petitioner’s ability to apply for the office did not arise solely from the challenged hereditary rule.
issues.conclusion: The petitioner was entitled to challenge the rule and the resulting appointment decision; his having applied did not bar the challenge.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished Bapatla Venkata Subba Rao v. Sikharam Ramakrishna Rao, where the claimant’s appointment claim depended on the very Act later challenged. Here, the petitioner had a right to apply independently of the hereditary preference, and the adverse orders applied that preference against him. The Court did not decide the general question whether a fundamental right can be waived.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenges_public_ap: A candidate brings a constitutional writ challenging a public appointment decision.
predicates.candidate_had_independent_right_to_apply: The candidate was entitled to apply for the office independently of the challenged preference.
predicates.adverse_decision_applied_descent_prefere: The decision adverse to the candidate relied on a preference based on descent.
predicates.candidate_may_challenge_descent_based_de: The candidate may challenge the descent-based decision despite having applied for the office.

issues.definition: If a candidate independently had the right to apply and an adverse public appointment decision applied a descent preference, the candidate may challenge that decision.
